explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says the commander released Paul before he brought him down to stand before the council. Acts 22:29 says the commander had bound him, so the chains were on his mind. That's an easy one to slip on, because chains are the detail that sticks.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The commander released Paul, then brought him down and had him stand before the council. He wanted to learn the real reason Paul was accused by the Jews. Being let out of a tight spot is a feeling I know well.

explanations.answer: His conscience has been good to this day
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says, “Brothers, I have conducted myself before God in all good conscience to this day.” Look at where he puts it: before God, not just before the council. That's a bold way to start when he's looking directly at the Sanhedrin.

explanations.answer: He has broken the law many times
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Paul says nothing like that in this passage. He says he has conducted himself before God in all good conscience to this day. That's a long way from owning up to a pile of broken laws.

explanations.answer: He has lived in fear of the council
explanations.explanation: Close to the mood, but not what Paul says. The text says he looked directly at the Sanhedrin. Then he said he has conducted himself before God in all good conscience to this day. Nothing about fear comes out of his mouth.

explanations.answer: high priest
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text calls Ananias the high priest. He's the one who ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. That's a heavy moment, and I think Paul felt it.

explanations.answer: commander
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. The commander is the one who brought Paul down and had the council assemble (Acts 22:30). The text calls Ananias the high priest, and he's the one who orders the strike. Two men with authority in one room, so I see how they got tangled.

explanations.answer: centurion
explanations.explanation: Not in this scene, friend. The text never calls Ananias a centurion. It says the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. The text gives him one title here, and it's high priest.

explanations.answer: By ordering that Paul be struck
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says, “You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law by commanding that I be struck.” His point is that the one judging by the law is the one who commanded the strike. A judge who breaks the rule while holding the rulebook is a hard thing to defend.

explanations.answer: By judging Paul on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The Sabbath never comes up in this passage. Paul names the command that Paul be struck as the law-breaking. Sticking to what the text says keeps us out of trouble.

explanations.answer: By taking money from the crowd
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. The text says nothing about money or a crowd paying anyone. Paul says the man violates the law by commanding that Paul be struck. That's the whole charge he names.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Paul replies, “I was not aware that he was the high priest…” Then he quotes what is written: “Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.” He answers the charge by pointing to Scripture.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Paul says, “I was not aware that he was the high priest…” That's what he tells the people who said, “How dare you insult the high priest of God!” So the text has Paul saying he didn't know.

explanations.answer: Speak evil about the ruler of your people
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul quotes what is written: “Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.” (Exodus 22:28) He says it right after the people nearby object to how he talked to the high priest. He brings the Word to the room, and that's a good way to answer.

explanations.answer: Bring your brother before the judges
explanations.explanation: Not that one, baker. Paul doesn't quote anything about bringing a brother before judges. He quotes, “Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.” (Exodus 22:28) The word brothers is how he addresses them, and I bet that's what made this one look right.

explanations.answer: Turn away from the elders of your people
explanations.explanation: Close in sound, but no. Paul's quote says, “Do not speak evil about the ruler of your people.” (Exodus 22:28) The Scripture is about speaking evil, not about turning away from anyone. This one is easy to mix up because the wording sounds alike.

explanations.answer: A dispute splits the Pharisees and Sadducees
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. As soon as Paul said it, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. One line from Paul and the room splits in two. I've seen a crowd argue over the last cookie, but not like this.

explanations.answer: The whole council calls for his death
explanations.explanation: Not what the text says, friend. It says a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. The council isn't calling for anything together. They're split.

explanations.answer: The high priest ends the meeting at once
explanations.explanation: Nope, baker. The text doesn't have the high priest ending anything. The assembly is divided, and later the commander is the one who orders soldiers to remove Paul. Nobody gets to call it quits quietly.

explanations.answer: The Sadducees say there is no resurrection
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Paul says he's on trial because of his hope in the resurrection of the dead. That's the exact spot where the two groups disagree.

explanations.answer: The Pharisees say Paul has left the law
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Later some scribes from the party of the Pharisees say, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” The split comes from what each group says about the resurrection. So the law isn't what the room is arguing over here.

explanations.answer: The Sadducees say Paul is no Pharisee
explanations.explanation: The text never says that, friend. Paul calls himself a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee, and the dispute comes from the resurrection. The Sadducees say there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits. That's the line the room splits on.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The Pharisees acknowledge them all: the resurrection, angels and spirits. The Sadducees say there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits. Same room, two different answers.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The text says the Sadducees say that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. So the Pharisees are the ones who say yes to all three. It's the Sadducees who say no.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The scribes from the party of the Pharisees say, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” That's the opposite of demanding punishment. It's easy to miss when a room is this loud.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The scribes from the party of the Pharisees get up and contend sharply, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” They aren't asking for punishment at all. For a moment, a few of them are on Paul's side.

explanations.answer: A spirit or an angel spoke to him
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. The scribes ask, “What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” They say it right after, “We find nothing wrong with this man.” It's a question, and the text leaves it as one.

explanations.answer: The Sadducees paid him to stir trouble
explanations.explanation: Nothing like that in the text, baker. The scribes ask, “What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” Money and payoffs never come up. It sounds juicy, but it isn't in the passage.

explanations.answer: The commander sent him to test them
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The commander called the council to learn the real reason Paul was accused. The scribes themselves wonder, “What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” Nobody in this text says Paul was sent to test them.

explanations.answer: barracks
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The commander orders the soldiers to go down, remove Paul by force and bring him into the barracks. The dispute grew so violent that he was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. That's a rough way to end the meeting, and I think it was a scary moment.

explanations.answer: temple
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. The commander orders the soldiers to bring Paul into the barracks, not the temple. The commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. So he ordered the soldiers to remove him by force.

explanations.answer: palace
explanations.explanation: Close, but no, baker. The text says the commander ordered the soldiers to bring Paul into the barracks. No palace in this scene. The dispute had grown so violent that he was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The Lord says, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.” He doesn't say it's finished. He says there is more testifying ahead.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The Lord stands near Paul and says, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.” Jerusalem isn't the end of it. Rome is still ahead.
